content: In sports, doping refers to the use of performance-enhancing drugs, particularly those prohibited by organizations that regulate competitions. Blood doping, another form of doping, involves either blood transfusions or the use of the hormone erythropoietin (EPO). Additionally, substances that mask other forms of doping are also considered doping by many. Most international sports organizations, including the International Olympic Committee, regard doping as unethical. This stance is based on concerns about the health risks of performance-enhancing drugs, the need to ensure equal opportunities for athletes, and the importance of promoting the exemplary image of clean sports to the public. Currently, substances like tetrahydrogestrinone (THG) and modafinil are at the center of doping controversies, with several high-profile cases involving prominent U.S. athletes testing positive for these substances. Some athletes who tested positive for modafinil argued that the drug was not on the prohibited list at the time of their offense. However, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) considers it a related substance to those already banned, and the decisions against these athletes have been upheld. Modafinil was officially added to the prohibited substances list on August 3, 2004, just ten days before the start of the 2004 Summer Olympics. In recent years, gene doping has emerged as a new form of doping. Gene doping is particularly concerning because it is difficult to detect and can result in permanent and irreversible changes. Sports lawyer Michelle Gallen has described the pursuit of doping athletes as akin to a modern-day witch hunt. The International Amateur Athletic Federation (now the International Association of Athletics Federations) was the first international sports governing body to address doping seriously. In 1928, they banned participants from doping, but due to the lack of testing methods, they relied on athletes' word that they were clean. It was not until 1966 that FIFA (soccer) and the Union Cycliste Internationale (cycling) joined the IAAF in combating drug use, followed by the International Olympic Committee the following year. Advances in pharmacology have often outpaced the ability of sports federations to implement effective testing procedures. However, since the establishment of the World Anti-Doping Agency in 1999, more athletes have been caught. The first drug tests for athletes were conducted at the 1966 European Championships, and in 1968, the IOC implemented drug testing at both the Summer and Winter Olympics. Anabolic steroids became widespread in the 1970s, and after a detection method was developed, they were added to the IOC's prohibited substances list in 1976. Some commentators argue that since completely preventing doping is impossible, all doping should be legalized. However, most experts disagree, citing the harmful long-term effects of many doping agents. If doping were legalized, all competitive athletes might feel compelled to use drugs, creating a level playing field but with widespread health consequences. Another perspective suggests that doping could be partially legalized through a drug whitelist and medical oversight to ensure safety, with all usage made public. However, under such a system, athletes might still cheat by exceeding official limits to gain an advantage, making enforcement as challenging as policing a total ban on performance-enhancing drugs. Historically, doping scandals have been prevalent in professional sports. As early as the late 19th century, professional cyclists used substances like caffeine, cocaine, and ether-coated sugar cubes to enhance performance, reduce pain, and delay fatigue. In the 1904 Olympics, marathon winner Thomas Hicks collapsed after taking brandy mixed with strychnine to secure his gold medal. In 1954, Soviet athletes at the World Weightlifting Championships reportedly used testosterone injections, leading to multiple gold medals and world records. In the early 1960s, Dr. John Ziegler administered Dianabol tablets to U.S. weightlifters, resulting in their dominance at the 1962 World Championships. The 1967 Tour de France saw cyclist Tom Simpson collapse and die during the ascent of Mont Ventoux, with amphetamines found in his possession. In the 1988 Summer Olympics, Canadian sprinter Ben Johnson won the 100m race but was later stripped of his gold medal after testing positive for stanozolol. He admitted to using multiple steroids and human growth hormone. During the 1970s and 1980s, many athletes from Eastern Bloc nations were suspected of using pharmacological aids to enhance their performance. In 1998, the Festina cycling team was excluded from the Tour de France after a team car was found carrying large quantities of performance-enhancing drugs. The team director admitted that some cyclists were routinely given banned substances. More recently, David Millar, the 2003 World Time Trial Champion, admitted to using EPO and was stripped of his title and suspended for two years. Roberto Heras was also stripped of his 2005 Vuelta a España victory after testing positive for EPO. At the 2001 FIS Nordic World Ski Championships, six Finnish cross-country skiers were disqualified for using Hemohes, a blood plasma expander. At the 2002 Winter Olympics, three Nordic skiers, including Johann Mühlegg, were caught doping and forfeited their medals. In 2006, the book Game of Shadows alleged extensive steroid use by baseball star Barry Bonds and other athletes. That same year, Spanish police uncovered a massive doping scheme involving top cyclists, leading to the withdrawal of several contenders from the 2006 Tour de France. The 2007 Tour de France was marred by multiple doping scandals. German rider Patrik Sinkewitz tested positive for elevated testosterone levels, and pre-race favorite Alexander Vinokourov tested positive for an illegal blood transfusion. Italian cyclist Cristian Moreni tested positive for testosterone, leading his entire Cofidis team to withdraw from the race. Race leader Michael Rasmussen was pulled from the Tour by his team for violating team rules, and Spanish rider Iban Mayo tested positive for EPO. In 2007, Tunisian swimmer Oussama Mellouli tested positive for amphetamines and received an 18-month competition ban. His results from the 2007 World Championships, including a gold medal in the 800m freestyle, were vacated. On October 5, 2007, track star Marion Jones admitted to using the steroid tetrahydrogestrinone (THG) and pled guilty to lying to federal agents about her drug use. The Anti-Doping Convention of the Council of Europe, opened for signature in 1989, was the first multilateral legal standard in this field. Signed by 48 states, including non-European countries like Australia and Canada, the Convention sets common standards and regulations for anti-doping measures. It requires parties to adopt legislative, financial, technical, and educational measures to combat doping. The Convention also established a Monitoring Group to oversee its implementation and periodically review the list of prohibited substances and methods. An Additional Protocol, effective in 2004, ensures mutual recognition of anti-doping controls and reinforces the Convention's implementation through a binding control system.
